title: Testing a Model
about: Find out how well a model really works by testing it fairly.

cards.prompt: A dog spotter scores **100%** on photos it trained on, answers included. Does that prove it's good?

options.text: No: it may just remember those exact photos
Yes: 100% means it got every single photo right
options.nudge: It did, on photos it had seen. Would a quiz you'd seen the answers to prove you learned?

options.text: Yes, as long as the test used lots of photos
options.nudge: More photos it has seen still only test memory. What photos show what it learned?

options.text: No: a model can never really score 100%
options.nudge: It can, on photos it has seen. What matters is which photos it was tested on.

cards.hint: Imagine a school test where you'd seen every question and answer the day before.
cards.explanation: A test it has already seen only checks its **memory**. To see what it really learned, test it on photos it has **never seen**.

cards.title: Keep some examples aside
cards.body:
So people split their examples. **Training examples** are for learning. **Test examples** are kept aside: the model never sees them while it learns.

**Accuracy** is the share of test examples it gets right: 8 out of 10 is 80%. A **fair test** uses new, realistic examples, easy and hard.

cards.prompt: A model is tested on **10** new photos and gets **7** right. What is its accuracy?
cards.hint: With 10 photos, each one is worth 10% of the test.
cards.nudge: Count only the photos it got right. Each of the 10 photos is worth 10%.
cards.explanation: Each photo is worth 10%, and it got 7 right: **70%**. The 3 it got wrong are the other 30%.

cards.prompt: Models can memorise training photos instead of learning. One scores **100%** on training, **60%** on new photos. Why?

options.text: The test photos were much harder than the training ones
options.nudge: Harder tests lower scores a bit, but a 40-point gap means something else.

options.text: It needs more training photos of exactly the same kind
options.nudge: More of the same makes it better at memorising. What does the gap show?

options.text: It's good: the 100% on training photos is what counts
options.nudge: Which score shows how it does on photos it has never seen?

options.text: It memorised its training photos, not the real pattern

cards.hint: Which score shows how it does on new photos? Why might the two differ?
cards.explanation: A big gap between training and test scores is the classic sign of **memorising instead of learning** ([[overfitting]]). The **test** score shows how it will really do.

cards.prompt: Is each one a **fair** test of how the model will really do, or an **unfair** one?

items.label: Examples kept aside from the start
A mix of easy and hard examples
Changing the test until it scores 100%

cards.hint: Which ones would make it look better than it really is?
cards.nudge: Look for tests that make the score look good without new, realistic examples.
cards.explanation: Fair tests use **unseen**, **realistic** examples, easy and hard. Its own training examples, only easy ones, or changing the test all make it look better than it is.

cards.prompt: A plant model will check gardeners' phone photos in sun, shade and rain. Which test is **fairest**?

options.text: 200 new phone photos from many gardens, in all weather
200 new photos taken by an expert, all in perfect light
options.nudge: They're new, but are they like the photos it will really meet?

options.text: 200 of its training photos, so the answers are known
options.nudge: Test photos need known answers too. What's wrong with ones it learned from?

options.text: 200 new phone photos it's already known to get right
options.nudge: Picking photos it gets right decides the score before the test.

cards.hint: A fair test is new and like real use. Check each option for both.
cards.explanation: Only the **new phone photos in all weather** are both unseen and realistic. Perfect-light photos flatter it, and the other two make the score meaningless.

cards.prompt: Label each training day from what really happened, then see how the model does on **4 new test days**.

examples.text: Thick cloud, wet air: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: Heavy cloud, damp evening: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: A few clouds, dry air: no rain
examples.label: dry

examples.text: Blue sky, slightly damp air: no rain
examples.label: dry

cards.hint: Each training day says what really happened: use that, not your own guess.
cards.nudge: Read the end of each training day again: it says whether it rained.
cards.explanation: Your labels were right. It got **3 of 4** test days right, but called the **cloudy but dry day** rain: every cloudy day it learned from was rainy.

cards.prompt: Add training days so the model gets **all 4** test days right.

examples.text: Thick cloud, wet air: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: Heavy cloud, damp evening: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: A few clouds, dry air: no rain
examples.label: dry

examples.text: Blue sky, slightly damp air: no rain
examples.label: dry

cards.hint: Which test day did it get wrong? Look for a new training day that's like it.
cards.nudge: Find a new day like the test it gets wrong, and check the others still pass.
cards.explanation: It had never seen a **cloudy but dry** day, so "Overcast, dry evening" fills that gap. The cloudy, damp night sits next to a rainy test day, so it breaks that one.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Keep **test examples** aside: the model never learns from them.
- **Accuracy** is the share it gets right: 8 of 10 is 80%.
- Perfect on training, poor on new examples? It memorised.

Next: when a model is unfair to some people.
